title: Interior Mutability

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
`Cell` and `RefCell` allow mutation behind an immutable outer binding. `RefCell` enforces the same shared-or-exclusive rule at runtime and panics if code violates it.

Normal Rust borrowing checks shared readers and exclusive writers at compile time. `RefCell<T>` moves that particular check to runtime for single-threaded code. An immutable binding can contain a `RefCell<Vec<_>>`, and calling `borrow_mut()` can still modify the vector inside. The outer reference is immutable; the cell enforces the inner access rule with a runtime borrow counter. It does not turn conflicting access into something safe to ignore.

In the sample, the temporary mutable guard from `borrow_mut()` ends after `push`, so a later `borrow()` is allowed. Keep a `RefMut` guard in a variable and try calling `borrow()` before dropping that guard: the program panics because a writer and reader would overlap. The fallible `try_borrow()` and `try_borrow_mut()` variants return an error instead of panicking, which can be useful when a conflict is a normal possibility. Hold guards for as short a period as practical.

`RefCell<T>` is not the tool for sharing mutable data across threads; types such as `Mutex<T>` address synchronization there. Use interior mutability when the surrounding API legitimately needs a shared outer reference while an inner value changes, such as a test spy or a local cache. Do not use it to escape a confusing borrow error before understanding the original ownership model. Runtime checks trade earlier compiler feedback for a more flexible access pattern, so that trade should be intentional.
